title: Fast means reading less

beats.say: How do you find one recipe in a library of a million books without reading them all?
You don't. You skip. First you walk to the right shelf, ignoring every other aisle. Then you glance at book spines, and pass over any that can't match.
Inside a book, you flip past chapters whose titles don't fit. And in a table, you read only the one column that answers you.

show.title: Keep skipping
items: Skip chapters that do not fit
Read only the column you need

beats.say: A database works the same way. Fast never means reading quicker. It means reading less. Each skip saves bytes, and bytes are the real cost.

check.q: What is the main way a query engine becomes faster on huge data?
opts: Reading the same bytes with a quicker reader
Skipping bytes it does not need to read
Copying all data into memory first
check.why: Time is spent reading and moving bytes, so the biggest win is to avoid reading bytes that cannot affect the answer.

work: Pick one slow query and write down how many bytes it scans.
Ask which shelf, spine, chapter and column it really needed.

title: Four levels of skipping

beats.say: Finance wants eighteen months of trips queried in under ten seconds. How do you scan three terabytes that fast?
You don't scan it. Level one: partitions. Data is foldered by date, so a one week question opens seven folders out of about five hundred and fifty.

Level two: files. Each file has minimum and maximum statistics, so files that cannot match are skipped. Level three: row groups. Each chunk of rows also stores a minimum and maximum, and the engine skips chunks outside your filter.
Level four: columns. Parquet stores columns separately, so a query naming two of forty columns reads about five percent. Stack the four skips and three terabytes becomes a few gigabytes.

check.q: A query uses 2 of 40 columns in a columnar file. Roughly how much column data is read?
opts: All of it
About half
About 5 percent
check.why: Columnar formats store each column separately, so only the named columns are read: 2 of 40 is 5 percent.

work: Name which of the four levels each of your big tables supports.
Run an explain on a date-filtered query and check bytes scanned.

title: Why pruning silently fails

beats.say: Why does a filter on a date sometimes still read every file?

Minimum and maximum only help if values are clustered. If every file holds trips from every day, each range covers everything, and nothing is skipped. Sorting or clustering on the filter column fixes that.
Wrapping the column in a function, like casting a timestamp to a string, can stop the engine comparing it with the statistics, so pruning silently fails. Filter on the raw column.

show.title: Keep the column bare
show.text:
bad:  where cast(pickup_ts as string) = '2025-03-01'
good: where pickup_ts >= '2025-03-01' and pickup_ts < '2025-03-02'

beats.say: Over-partitioning hurts too. Partitioning by user creates millions of folders and tiny files, and listing them costs more than the data you skipped. A table format keeps file statistics in one manifest, so there is no listing.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Too many partitions means tiny files

check.q: Every file contains rows from every day, and you filter on one day. What happens?
opts: Min/max skips most files
Almost no files are skipped
The engine errors out
check.why: Each file's range spans all days, so no file can be excluded. Clustering by date makes ranges narrow.

work: Check whether your filter columns are sorted or clustered within files.
Search queries for functions wrapped around partition or filter columns.
Count files per partition and compact tiny ones.

title: Choosing a layout

beats.say: If skipping bytes is everything, why not partition and sort on every column?

Because every layout favors one question. Partition by date and date queries fly, but a query by driver still touches every folder. Pick the column most queries filter on, with a few hundred to thousands of values.

Use partitions for coarse cuts, and sorting or clustering inside files for the rest. A table format adds file statistics, so you skip files without listing folders. The price is compaction jobs that rewrite small files.
Don't bother under a few gigabytes; just scan. For single-row lookups, use a key-value store. And on pay-per-byte engines, fewer bytes read is a smaller bill.

check.q: Most queries filter by date, some by driver. Which layout is best?
opts: Partition by driver
Partition by date, cluster by driver inside files
Partition by date and driver together
check.why: Date has few values, so it suits partitions. Driver has many values, so clustering avoids millions of tiny partitions while still narrowing ranges.

work: Review the top ten queries and pick the layout key from their filters.
Schedule compaction and track average file size.
Skip tuning for tables under a few gigabytes.

title: Drawers and pigeonholes

beats.say: How do you find one day's receipts in a warehouse holding ten years of paper? You certainly don't open every box.
Partitioning means labeling one drawer for each day. Ask for October eleventh, and you open one drawer and ignore the rest. Skipping drawers is called pruning, and it saves the most work.
But don't label a drawer per customer. Five million customers means five million nearly empty drawers, and walking between them takes forever.
For customers, use sorting pigeonholes instead. Give every name a number from one to sixteen, and always drop it in the same hole. Now one customer's mail lives in one place.

check.q: Which column is the better choice for labeling drawers, meaning partitioning?
opts: Customer id, with millions of values
Date, with a few hundred values
A random number for each row
check.why: Drawers only help when there are few of them and you ask for them by label. Date fits. Customer id would create millions of nearly empty drawers.

work: List the columns your biggest tables are filtered on most often.
Count how many distinct values each of those columns has.
Name one column that would make far too many drawers.

title: How pruning and buckets work

beats.say: A query asks for one day of trips. How does the engine avoid reading a whole year of data?

The table is split into directories, one per date value, like dt equals 2026-10-11. The query filter matches one directory name, so the engine lists only that folder. Three hundred sixty-five days becomes one. That is partition pruning.
Bucketing handles columns with millions of values. The engine hashes rider id, then takes the remainder after dividing by sixteen. That remainder picks one of sixteen files in each partition.
If two tables use the same bucket count on the join key, bucket five meets bucket five directly. No shuffle, which means no sending data across the network.

check.q: Two tables are both bucketed on rider id with 16 buckets. What does the engine gain on a join by rider id?
opts: It can join matching buckets directly without a shuffle
It can skip all partitions
It no longer needs to read any files
check.why: Matching rows are guaranteed to sit in the same bucket number in both tables, so each pair joins locally. Files still get read, and partition pruning is a separate feature.

work: Check whether your daily big join could use matching bucketed tables.
Open a query plan and find the shuffle step on the join.
Confirm which tables are partitioned by date today.

title: Where partitioning bites back

beats.say: Why can a partitioned table end up slower than an unpartitioned one?

Because each partition should hold at least hundreds of megabytes. Partition by rider id and you get five million directories of tiny files. Listing them and opening each file costs more than reading the data.
Pruning also only works if the query filters on the partition column. Filter on a different column and the engine reads every directory.

Bucketing has its own trap. The bucket count is fixed at write time. Join a sixteen bucket table to a thirty-two bucket one, and the engine may shuffle after all. Both tables must be bucketed the same way.

check.q: A table is partitioned by date, but most queries filter only on city. What happens?
opts: Pruning works because date is a partition column
The engine reads every date directory
The engine builds buckets automatically
check.why: Pruning needs a filter on the partition column. Without a date filter, every directory is read.

work: Check the average file size in each partition and flag any under 100 megabytes.
Compare how many buckets each joined table uses.
Review whether query filters match the partition column.

title: Choosing partitions or buckets

beats.say: Partition by date and bucket by rider. Is that always the right call?
Rule of thumb: partition by what you filter on with low cardinality. Bucket by what you join on with high cardinality.
Partitioning is cheap and gives the biggest saving, so start there. But every extra partition column multiplies directories. Date plus city plus device can explode into millions.

Bucketing costs more. Writers must hash and sort, the count is baked in, and growth means rewriting. Use it for a join repeated daily on the same key, or for rider lookups. For a one-off join, a shuffle is cheaper than the commitment.

show.title: Bucket only when it pays
items: Changing the count means a rewrite

check.q: A team joins two huge tables on rider id once a quarter. What is the sensible choice?
opts: Bucket both tables on rider id with 16 buckets
Partition both tables by rider id
Accept the shuffle for that rare job
check.why: Bucketing adds write cost and a fixed layout. For a rare join, one shuffle costs less than that commitment, and partitioning by rider id would create millions of tiny files.

work: Review the table layouts and mark each as filter-driven or join-driven.
Bucket only the joins that run daily on the same key.
Set a minimum partition size target and alert when files fall below it.

title: The catalog and the boxes

beats.say: Imagine a warehouse with a million boxes and no labels. How do you find last Tuesday's invoices?
You keep a catalog book at the front desk. For each shelf it says what the boxes hold, what the columns mean, and where to walk. That book is the metastore. The boxes are just files.
Shelves are grouped by date, so a question about Tuesday walks to one shelf only. Nobody checks a box when it is put away. The catalog's description is applied only when you open it.

chip.text: Checked on opening, not on storing

beats.say: Throw away the catalog entry and the boxes stay, if the shelf is external. If the warehouse owns the boxes, they are shredded too. So for shared data, keep it external.

show.title: Who owns the boxes?
items: External: drop removes only the catalog entry
Managed: drop shreds the files too

check.q: You drop an external table. What happens to its files?
opts: They are deleted
They stay; only the catalog entry goes
They are moved to a trash folder
check.why: An external table only has a metastore entry that Hive owns. The files belong to you, so dropping removes just the catalog record.

work: List which of your lake tables are managed and which are external.
Make shared lake tables external before anyone runs a drop.
Write down who owns each table's storage folder.

title: How a Hive query finds its files

beats.say: When you run a query on a Hive table, where does the engine learn which files to read?
It asks the metastore, a small database. For a sales table it returns the schema, the location, and the partition list, like date equals 2026-11-01.
Now filter on one date. The engine prunes the other 364 partitions and lists only that directory, maybe 200 files. Without the filter it reads all 365 days. Pruning is the whole speed trick.
Then it opens the files and applies the schema while reading. That is schema-on-read. A bad row is not rejected on write. It shows up as a null or an error at query time.

check.q: Why does filtering on the partition column make a query faster?
opts: The engine prunes partitions and lists only matching directories
The metastore caches the results
The files are compressed more
check.why: Partition values live in the directory path, so the engine can skip whole folders without opening them.

work: Check that your biggest queries filter on the partition column.
Look at an explain plan and count the partitions scanned.
Add a check at write time, since nothing validates files for you.

title: Half-written partitions and slow planning

beats.say: A job writes 200 files, fails after 120. What does a reader see?

Half a partition. Hive has no atomic commit across files, so readers see the 120 files as if they were complete. Totals are silently wrong. The usual fix is writing to a temporary directory and swapping it in, but that swap is still not atomic on object storage.

Planning has a cost too. The engine lists every partition directory, and on object storage each list call is a slow network request. With 100,000 partitions, planning can take minutes before any data is read.
Last gotcha: drift. Files copied in outside Hive are invisible until you run M S C K repair table, which registers the new partitions.

check.q: A copy tool drops a new date folder straight into storage. Queries do not see it. Why?
opts: Schema-on-read rejects the files
The metastore does not list that partition yet
The engine caches old file sizes
check.why: The partition list lives in the metastore. Folders added outside Hive stay invisible until registered, for example with MSCK REPAIR TABLE.

work: Register new partitions as the last step of every ingest job.
Write to a temporary location and publish only after success.
Track partition counts per table and alert when they climb.

title: Drop, update and repartition traps

beats.say: Someone runs drop table on a table. Did you just lose a year of data?

It depends on the type. For a managed table, Hive owns the files, so drop deletes them. For an external table, only the metastore entry goes, and the files stay. That is why lake data should almost always be external.
Two more limits. Updating one row means rewriting its whole partition, maybe gigabytes, because files are never edited in place.

show.title: No row-level changes
items: Fix one row, rewrite the partition

beats.say: And the partition scheme is frozen. Moving from daily to hourly means rewriting the whole table, since the directory layout is the partitioning.

check.q: You must correct one wrong row in a 5 GB Hive partition. What is required?
opts: Edit the row in place
Rewrite the partition's files
Update the metastore entry only
check.why: Hive tables are plain immutable files with no row-level changes, so the fix means rewriting the partition.

work: Audit tables for managed type and convert to external.
Keep partitions sized so a rewrite is affordable.
Choose partition granularity carefully before data lands.

title: When to leave Hive tables behind

beats.say: Your team wants a new lake table. Do you reach for Hive tables?
Rarely, for new builds. The Hive layout is cheap and every engine reads it, so it is fine for append-only, rarely changing data, like raw landing zones and logs.

But it breaks where you need updates, deletes, concurrent writers or reliable reads during writes. Table formats like Iceberg and Delta keep a transaction log of files, which gives atomic commits, and avoid directory listing.
Even then, the metastore often stays as the catalog, so engines can find tables. Choose by write pattern, not habit, and plan migration before partitions pass tens of thousands.

show.title: Decision rule
items: Migrate before partitions hit tens of thousands

check.q: Which workload most clearly justifies moving off plain Hive tables?
opts: Append-only clickstream logs
Frequent row updates with concurrent writers
A table queried by one engine
check.why: Updates and concurrent writers need atomic commits and row-level changes, which table formats provide and Hive layout lacks.

work: Classify tables by write pattern: append-only or mutable.
Pilot Iceberg or Delta on your most update-heavy table.
Set a partition count threshold that triggers migration review.

title: Rows or columns: the phone book

beats.say: Imagine a phone book with ten million people. You only want the list of everyone's city. How much of the book must you read?
A row format is the normal phone book. Each person's name, city and fare sit together on one line. Great when you want one whole person. But for just the city, you must flip through every page.

A column format is a book regrouped. One section holds only cities, another only fares. Want cities? Open one section and ignore the rest. That is why analytics, which touches a few columns, loves it.
The catch: rebuilding one whole person means visiting every section. So columns suit reading, rows suit writing records one by one.

show.title: The trade
items: Columns: fast to read a few fields across many records
Rows: fast to write or fetch one whole record

check.q: A query totals one column across millions of records. Which layout reads the least data?
opts: Row format
Column format
They read the same amount
check.why: A column format keeps all values of one column together, so the reader opens just that section and skips the rest.

work: List the five most common queries on your biggest table and count how many columns each touches.
Check whether your analytics tables are stored in a row format such as CSV or JSON.

title: Inside a Parquet file

beats.say: A query needs 5 columns out of 80. How does a Parquet file let you read only those, and skip most of the rows too?

A file is split into row groups, about 128 megabytes each. Inside each group, every column is stored as its own chunk. At the end sits a footer with the schema and, for every chunk, its minimum, maximum and null count.

The reader opens the footer first. It learns where each chunk starts, so it fetches just the five columns it needs. That is column pruning. Reading five of eighty means roughly a sixteenth of the bytes.
Now filter fare greater than 5000. If a row group's maximum fare is 900, nothing inside can match, so the reader skips it entirely. That is predicate pushdown.

check.q: What lets a reader skip a row group without reading its data?
opts: The min and max statistics in the footer
A sorted file name
The dictionary of each page
check.why: The footer records min, max and null count per column chunk, so if the filter value falls outside that range the group cannot contain a match.

work: Open a Parquet footer with a tool such as parquet-tools and read the row group statistics.
Compare bytes scanned for a query selecting five columns versus select star.

title: Why columns compress so well

beats.say: A city column holds ten million values but only ten different cities. How small can that get?
Because similar values sit together, Parquet builds a dictionary. Each city name becomes a small number, zero to nine. Instead of repeating a long string, the file stores a tiny integer.
Next comes run-length encoding. If the same city repeats a million times in a row, the file stores the pair: city three, one million times. Just two numbers.
But runs only form if equal values are neighbours. So sort by city before writing. Sorting also tightens each group's minimum and maximum, which makes pushdown skip far more. Sort once, win twice.

show.title: Sort before you write
items: Equal values sit together, so runs get long
Tight min and max per group, so more skipping

check.q: Why does sorting by a column before writing Parquet help?
opts: It makes the footer smaller
It groups equal values for run-length encoding and tightens min and max statistics
It turns the file into a row format
check.why: Sorted data forms long runs that compress well and gives each row group a narrow value range, so pushdown can skip more groups.

work: Pick the column most often used in filters and sort the table by it on write.
Compare file size and scan time before and after sorting one table.

title: When Parquet pruning fails

beats.say: Your Parquet table has min and max statistics, yet the query still reads every row group. Why?

show.sub: why does the query read everything?

beats.say: Statistics only help when values are clustered. If fares are random, every group spans from 1 to 9000, so no group can be ruled out. Unsorted data quietly turns pushdown into a full scan.

show.title: Random data: every group looks alike

beats.say: The opposite trap is tiny files. A streaming job writing a file every minute makes thousands of small files. Each one needs its own footer read and a storage request, and row groups far under 128 megabytes waste the layout. Compact them regularly.

Also remember: a column where almost every value is different, like event id, gets no useful dictionary, so it compresses poorly. And a footer lives at the end, so a writer must finish the file before anyone can read it.

show.title: Two more gotchas
items: Nearly unique columns, like event id, compress poorly
The footer is written last, so unfinished files are unreadable

check.q: A table's queries filter on fare but still scan every row group. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Fares are scattered randomly, so each group's min and max cover the whole range
Parquet does not support filters
The footer is missing the schema
check.why: Min and max only rule out a group when its range excludes the filter value. Random data makes every range wide, so nothing is skipped.

work: Check the average file size in your largest table and schedule compaction if it is far below 128 MB.
Cluster or sort data by the main filter column when you write it.

title: Why Avro for messages

beats.say: Why would you pick a row format for Kafka messages when columns compress so well?
Messages arrive one at a time. A columnar file needs a batch to build column chunks and a footer, so writing one record at a time is slow. Avro just appends each record whole, which is fast.

Avro also carries its schema with the data. The writer's schema says how the bytes were written; the reader's schema says what the consumer wants. Clear rules resolve the two, so adding a field with a default won't break old readers.

chip.text: New field with default is safe

beats.say: The cost: to total one column, Avro must read every whole record. So land data as Avro, then convert to Parquet for analytics.

check.q: Which change is safe under Avro schema resolution?
opts: Adding a new field with a default value
Renaming a field with no alias
Changing a string field to a map
check.why: A new field with a default lets readers fill in the value for older data, so compatibility holds. Renames without aliases and type changes break resolution.

work: Check which compatibility mode your schema registry enforces for your key topics.
Add a job that converts landed Avro into Parquet for analysts.

title: Choosing a file format

beats.say: Parquet, ORC or Avro? The answer has two halves.

For analytics tables in a lake, choose columnar, and default to Parquet. It is supported by nearly every engine, handles nested types, and avoids lock-in. Choose ORC only if your estate is centred on Hive, where its built-in indexes pay off.

show.title: Analytics: columnar
items: Default to Parquet: pruning, pushdown, support everywhere

beats.say: For records moving between systems one at a time, choose Avro, for fast writes and enforced schema compatibility. JSON and CSV are fine for exchange with outside parties, but never for large analytics: they are text, have no pruning, and compress badly.

show.title: Movement: row
items: Avro for Kafka and landing zones
JSON and CSV only for outside exchange

beats.say: So the architecture is usually both: Avro at the edges where data arrives, Parquet in the lake where it is queried. Don't use columnar for tiny, record-by-record lookups, and budget for compaction jobs.

check.q: You are designing an estate with Kafka ingestion and a lake queried by analysts. What do you choose?
opts: Parquet everywhere, including Kafka messages
Avro for messages and landing, Parquet for lake tables
CSV for both, for simplicity
check.why: Avro suits fast single-record writes with strict schema rules, while Parquet suits analytic reads through pruning, pushdown and compression.

work: Write a one-page format decision note stating where each of Avro and Parquet is used and why.
Estimate compaction cost for your streaming tables before choosing write frequency.

title: Why tiny files are slow

beats.say: Why would ten thousand tiny files take hundreds of times longer to read than one big file holding the same data?

show.sub: same data, hundreds of times slower

beats.say: Picture moving house. One big box takes one trip. Ten thousand envelopes mean ten thousand trips, and each one needs a door opened and a label read.

chip.text: Trips, not data, cost the time

beats.say: A data lake works the same way. Every file costs a request to open, a footer to read, and a line in the catalog. Tiny files make the overhead bigger than the actual reading.
The fix is compaction: tipping the envelopes into a few big boxes. Same data, far fewer trips.

show.sub: many small files become a few big ones

check.q: Why are many tiny files slower to scan than one large file with the same data?
opts: Tiny files hold more data
Each file adds fixed overhead like opening and reading a footer
Large files are compressed and small files are not
check.why: The data volume is the same. The extra time is fixed per-file overhead repeated thousands of times.

work: Count the files and total size of your busiest table.
Ask which jobs write to it and how often.

title: Where small files come from, and the four jobs

beats.say: Ten thousand 50 kilobyte files, or one 500 megabyte file. Same data, so why is one hundreds of times slower to scan?
Each file needs a request to open and a footer read. Ten thousand files means ten thousand requests, mostly waiting, not reading.
They come from three places: streaming micro-batches writing every few seconds, partitions sliced too fine, and Spark writing one file per shuffle partition into every table partition.

show.title: Three sources
items: One file per shuffle partition per table partition

beats.say: Iceberg gives four housekeeping jobs. Rewrite data files compacts small files. Expire snapshots drops old versions. Remove orphan files deletes strays. Rewrite manifests tidies the metadata.

check.q: Which write pattern most directly creates small files?
opts: Streaming micro-batches committing every few seconds
One nightly batch load of 500 MB
Running expire snapshots
check.why: Each frequent commit writes a small file, so the file count grows quickly.

work: List which of your tables get micro-batch writes.
Schedule the four Iceberg jobs in an Airflow DAG per table.

title: Why compaction does not free space yet

beats.say: You compacted a table, so why did your storage bill go up?

show.sub: the old files are still there

beats.say: Compaction writes new big files and a new snapshot. But older snapshots still point at the old small files, so nothing can be deleted yet. For a while you store both.
Space comes back only after expire snapshots runs. But expiring also ends time travel to those versions. So retention is a business decision: how far back might anyone need to roll back or audit?
Remove orphan files cleans up files no snapshot knows about, such as leftovers from failed writes. Use an age threshold, so you never delete a file from a write still in progress.

show.title: Orphan files
items: Only delete files older than a safe age

check.q: After rewrite_data_files finishes, when does storage actually shrink?
opts: Immediately
After expire_snapshots removes snapshots referencing the old files
After rewrite_manifests runs
check.why: Older snapshots still reference the small files, so they stay until those snapshots expire.

work: Agree a snapshot retention period with the data owners.
Run orphan removal with an age threshold, never zero.

title: Prevent small files, do not just mop them

beats.say: Is nightly compaction the real fix for small files, or just a mop?

It is a mop. Prevent at write time. Let adaptive query execution coalesce shuffle partitions, and route all rows for one table partition to one task before writing. Each partition then gets a few large files.
Also question the partitioning. Partitions that are too fine multiply files however well you write. Choose coarser partitions, such as day instead of minute.

Keep maintenance as scheduled Airflow jobs, since compaction costs compute and rewrites data. Streaming tables need it more often. Set retention with the business, balancing audit needs against storage cost.

show.title: Maintenance trade-offs
items: Streaming tables need it more often

check.q: What is the best primary strategy against small files?
opts: Compact more often
Avoid creating them: coalesce shuffle partitions, route rows per partition, partition coarser
Delete old snapshots daily
check.why: Prevention avoids paying compute to rewrite data; compaction stays as a safety net.

work: Review Spark write jobs for shuffle partition count and routing.
Report files per partition and average file size on key tables.

title: A rulebook beside the files

beats.say: Your data lake is just a pile of files. So how can two people change it at once without breaking it?

A table format is a rulebook sitting beside the files. It records which files make up the table right now. Delta Lake keeps a numbered receipt for every change. Hudi keeps an index, like a filing cabinet label for each record. Iceberg keeps a catalogue, like a library.
Readers trust the rulebook, not the folder. A change is either fully written down or it never happened. That is what atomic means.

show.sub: Atomic means a change is fully recorded or not at all

check.q: What does a table format add on top of a pile of data files?
opts: A faster disk
A record of which files make up the table, so changes are all or nothing
A way to compress files into one
check.why: The format is a rulebook of metadata. Readers follow it instead of listing the folder, so a half-finished write is never seen.

work: Explain to a colleague why a plain folder of Parquet files cannot give atomic changes.
List which of your tables are plain files and which sit under a table format.

title: How Delta Lake replays its log

beats.say: How does Delta Lake know what your table looks like right now?

show.text: What is the table right now?

beats.say: Every write adds a numbered JSON file to the delta log folder: zero zero zero one, zero zero zero two, and so on. Each file lists data files added and removed.

To read the table, replay the log from the start. That gets slow after thousands of commits, so every ten commits Delta writes a Parquet checkpoint. Readers load the latest checkpoint, then replay only the few newer files.
Time travel is just replaying to an older number.

show.sub: Replay the log up to commit 7

check.q: Why does Delta write a checkpoint every ten commits?
opts: So readers skip replaying the whole log from commit one
So old data files can be deleted
So two writers never conflict
check.why: A checkpoint is a Parquet snapshot of table state. Readers start from it and replay only newer commits, keeping reads fast.

work: Open a Delta table's log folder and find the latest checkpoint file.
Query an older version of a table and note which commit number you used.

title: Hudi keys, and Iceberg trees

beats.say: Why was Hudi built at Uber? Because millions of trip records changed every day.

show.sub: Trips change after they are written

beats.say: Hudi gives every record a key and keeps an index from key to file. An update goes straight to the right file, with no scan of the whole table.

Copy on write rewrites the whole file on each update, so reads are fast but writes cost more. Merge on read appends changes to a small log file and merges later, so writes are fast but reads do extra work.
Iceberg instead uses a tree of metadata files, so engines can skip data without listing folders.

check.q: A Hudi table gets constant small updates and must write quickly. Which type fits best?
opts: Copy on write, because it rewrites whole files
Merge on read, because it appends changes and merges later
Neither, Hudi cannot do updates
check.why: Merge on read makes writes cheap by appending to log files. You pay later at read time or at compaction.

work: Pick one update-heavy table and estimate how often a typical file would be rewritten under copy on write.
Decide what read delay your users can tolerate before choosing merge on read.

title: Conflicts, compaction and vacuum

beats.say: What happens when two writers commit to a Delta table at the same moment?

Delta uses optimistic concurrency. Both try to write the next numbered file, say number forty two. The storage layer lets only one create it. The loser checks whether the winner touched the same files. If not, it retries as number forty three. If yes, it fails.

Gotchas. Merge on read tables need regular compaction, or reads slow down as log files pile up. Vacuum deletes old data files, and then time travel to those versions breaks. Many tiny commits also create small files, which make every query slower.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Compact merge on read tables or reads slow down
Vacuum removes old files and ends time travel to them
Tiny commits create small files and slow queries

check.q: You ran vacuum with a short retention, and now a query on last week's version fails. Why?
opts: The checkpoint was corrupted
The data files for that version were physically deleted
Optimistic concurrency rolled it back
check.why: The log still names the version, but vacuum removed the data files it points to, so time travel cannot read them.

work: Check the vacuum retention on your tables against how far back you need time travel.
Schedule compaction and watch file counts per table.

title: Choosing a format without picking a winner

beats.say: Delta, Hudi or Iceberg: which one wins? Wrong question.

All three give atomic commits, time travel and row level changes. So the choice follows your engines. Delta where Databricks is the centre. Iceberg where Spark, Trino, Flink and Snowflake must share the same tables. Hudi where record level upserts dominate the workload.

The formats are converging. Snowflake and Databricks now both read and write Iceberg. So the cost of a wrong choice is shrinking. Do not overthink the decision. Pick for today's engines, and keep data in open files so you can change later.

show.title: Decision rules
items: Same core features in all three
Formats are converging on Iceberg support
Pick for today's engines, keep data in open files

check.q: Five teams on Spark, Trino, Flink and Snowflake must share tables. What is the strongest reasoning?
opts: Pick Hudi because it is fastest
Pick Iceberg because wide engine support matters most when many engines share tables
Pick whichever format is newest
check.why: All three cover the core features, so engine support decides. Iceberg is read and written by the widest range of engines.

work: List every engine that reads or writes your core tables before debating formats.
Write a one paragraph decision note that ties the format to engines, not features.

title: A form instead of a letter

beats.say: Why can't a program act on a paragraph written by an AI? Because a program needs boxes to look in, not a letter to read.

chip.text: Prose has no boxes to branch on

beats.say: Picture a hospital. A patient can ramble about their pain for ten minutes. So the nurse hands over a form: pick a type, tick urgent or not, write one line of proof. Now the system knows where to send them.
Structured output is that form for a model. You define the boxes, and you forbid chatting, so the model can only fill them in. A pipeline can then retry, page someone, or route the failure.
Then a clerk checks the form. Is every box filled with an allowed choice? If not, it goes back. And one box says unknown, so odd cases are not squeezed into the wrong answer.

chip.text: Odd cases get an honest label

check.q: Why does the form include an unknown box?
opts: So the model can skip hard work
So odd cases are not forced into a wrong category
So the form looks longer
So the clerk can skip checking
check.why: Without an escape value, every unfamiliar case must be squeezed into the nearest wrong box, and your routing would act on a wrong label.

work: Find one place where your pipeline reads model prose, and list the fields it really needs.
Add an unknown or other value to every closed list of categories you ask a model to pick from.

title: Forcing a model to fill a schema

beats.say: How do you make a model return fields instead of prose? You hand it a fake tool.

show.sub: It exists only to force fields

beats.say: Define a Pydantic class with four fields: category, retryable, evidence line, and confidence between zero and one. Turn it into a JSON schema and register it as a tool. Nothing runs. The tool is only a form.

Next, set tool choice to that tool's name. Now the model cannot reply with text. It must return arguments matching the schema. Send a log tail, and a small, cheap model answers in under four hundred tokens.

Last, validate. Pydantic checks every field. If it fails, send the error back as a tool result, and let the model try again. After two attempts, return unknown, not retryable, so the pipeline never crashes.

items: Fail: send error back, retry once

check.q: What does setting tool choice to the named tool accomplish?
opts: It runs the tool on your server
It makes the model reply only with arguments matching the schema
It guarantees the answer is true
It makes the model cheaper
check.why: Tool choice removes the option of a text reply, so the model must produce arguments in your schema's shape. Nothing runs and truth is not guaranteed, which is why you still validate.

work: Write the Pydantic model first, then generate the tool's input schema from it so the two never drift.
Cap retries at two and make the fallback a safe value such as unknown and not retryable.

title: Valid does not mean true

beats.say: The output passed validation, so why might it still be wrong?

Because a schema checks shape, not truth. A model can pick a valid category that is simply the wrong one, and invent a log line that sounds right. So you ask for the evidence line copied exactly, then check mechanically that it appears in the input. If not, discard the answer.

Second, the closed list needs an unknown value. Without it, a new failure type gets forced into the nearest wrong bucket, and a wrong retry can loop for hours. Also, confidence is the model's own guess, so treat it as a hint, not a probability.

show.title: Two quiet traps
items: No unknown value: new failures land in the wrong bucket
A wrong bucket can trigger endless retries

beats.say: Third, retries are bounded. Feed the validation error back, try twice, then fall back to unknown. Never retry forever, and never let a malformed answer reach your router.

check.q: The model returns a schema-valid answer whose evidence line is not in the log. What should you do?
opts: Accept it because it validated
Raise its confidence threshold
Discard it, because the evidence is not in the input
Add more categories
check.why: Validation proves shape, not truth. An evidence line absent from the log shows the answer is made up, so discard it and retry or fall back.

work: Add a mechanical check that the evidence line appears in the input, and count how often it fails.
Never route on the confidence field alone; treat it as a hint and measure real accuracy on labeled failures.

title: When structured output earns its place

beats.say: When is a schema the wrong tool, and when is a small model the wrong choice?

show.sub: Right for triage, wrong for open reasoning

beats.say: Use forced structured output when code must branch on the result and the volume is high. Classifying thousands of failed tasks a day on a small, cheap model costs little and is fast. But a rigid schema hurts open-ended reasoning, because the model has no room to think.

So split the work. The cheap model triages every failure into a category. Only unknown or low-trust cases go to a stronger model for root-cause analysis, where free text is fine. Also, if a plain rule can match an out-of-memory error, use a regex and skip the model entirely.

chip.text: Spend big-model cost only on the hard few

beats.say: Plan for drift. Log every category, validation failure and discarded answer, so you notice when a new failure type appears and your list needs a new value.

show.title: Watch for drift
items: Track validation failures and discarded answers
A rising unknown rate means add a category

check.q: What is the best design for classifying thousands of failures a day and also explaining the hard ones?
opts: One strong model with free text for everything
A small model with a schema for triage, a stronger model only for hard cases
Regex only, no model
A small model for everything, including root cause
check.why: Triage is simple and high volume, so a small model with a schema is cheap and branchable. Hard, open-ended cases deserve a stronger model with room to reason.

work: Measure the unknown rate weekly and treat a rise as a signal to review your categories.
Move any failure pattern a simple rule can catch out of the model path to cut cost and latency.

title: A table is a card catalog

beats.say: How can a huge pile of files act like one tidy table, without anyone walking every shelf?

show.sub: How does a pile become a table?

beats.say: Think of a library. The books are the data files. Instead of searching every shelf, you use the card catalog. It says which shelf, and which books cover your topic.
Iceberg keeps that catalog as small files of notes. One note points to the latest list. That list points to groups of books. Each group notes what is inside every book.

show.title: Notes about notes
items: One pointer to the latest note
A list of groups of books

beats.say: When the librarian adds books, she writes a fresh catalog, then swaps one sign at the front desk. Visitors see the old catalog or the new one, never a half-written mess. Old catalogs stay around, so you can ask what the library looked like last Tuesday.

check.q: In the library analogy, what does the single swap at the front desk give you?
opts: Faster shelves
Readers see the old catalog or the new one, never a half-written one
Books get deleted automatically
check.why: Swapping one pointer is atomic, so readers never see a partly updated table.

work: Explain Iceberg to a colleague using the catalog analogy.
List which of your tables would benefit from asking what it looked like last week.

title: How a query reads the metadata tree

beats.say: How does Iceberg answer a query over billions of rows without listing a single folder?

show.sub: Billions of rows, zero directory scans

beats.say: The catalog holds one pointer to the current metadata file. That file lists the schema, the partition spec, and every snapshot. The current snapshot points to a manifest list.
The manifest list has partition ranges, so you skip manifests that miss your filter. Each surviving manifest has one row per data file: path, row count, and the minimum and maximum of every column.

show.title: Two rounds of pruning
items: Manifest: min and max per column
Both prune before any data is read

beats.say: Filter on one day. Out of ten thousand files, the statistics might leave forty. The engine opens only those forty Parquet files. Listing ten thousand objects on cloud storage is slow. Reading a few small metadata files is not.

check.q: What lets Iceberg skip a data file without opening it?
opts: A directory listing
Per-file column minimum and maximum stored in manifests
The file name's date
check.why: Manifests store row counts and column min and max per file, so the planner rules out files from metadata alone.

work: Run a query on the snapshots and files metadata tables of one of your tables.
Check whether your common filter columns have useful min and max spread.

title: Commits, races and retries

beats.say: What happens when two writers commit to the same Iceberg table at the same moment?
A write first creates new data files, new manifests, and a new metadata file. Nothing is visible yet. Then it asks the catalog to swap the pointer from the old metadata file to the new one.

The swap is atomic, so readers see the old snapshot or the new one, never half. If two writers race, one swap fails. That writer rereads the winner's commit and retries on top. This is optimistic concurrency: no locks, just retry.
The gotchas. Old snapshots and files pile up until you expire them, and time travel works only while snapshots exist. Many writers on one table can cause retry storms.

check.q: Two writers race to commit. What happens to the loser?
opts: The table is corrupted
Its swap fails and it retries on top of the winner's commit
Readers see half of each write
check.why: Optimistic concurrency lets one atomic swap win; the other rebases on the new state and retries.

work: Schedule snapshot expiry and orphan file cleanup.
Count concurrent writers per hot table and look for commit retries in logs.

title: Copy-on-write or merge-on-read

beats.say: You change one row inside a ten gigabyte file. Do you rewrite ten gigabytes?
With copy-on-write, yes. Every data file holding a changed row is rewritten. Writes are expensive, but reads stay fast because files are clean.
With merge-on-read, no. Iceberg writes a small delete file marking removed rows, plus the new rows. Writes are cheap. But every read must merge those deletes until compaction cleans them up.

So pick by pattern. Occasional batch changes, read all day: copy-on-write. Frequent small changes, like a change data capture feed: merge-on-read, with compaction scheduled. Skip compaction and reads slowly decay.

check.q: A change data capture feed updates thousands of rows every minute. Which mode fits best?
opts: Copy-on-write
Merge-on-read with scheduled compaction
Neither, rewrite the table nightly
check.why: Frequent small changes make copy-on-write rewrites too costly; delete files are cheap, and compaction keeps reads fast.

work: Check which mode each of your update-heavy tables uses.
Add a compaction job and alert on delete file counts.

title: What Iceberg costs you

beats.say: Iceberg gives you atomic commits and time travel on plain files. What does it cost you?

Metadata becomes something you operate. Snapshots, manifests and small files grow with every commit. You need scheduled expiry, manifest rewrites and file compaction, or planning slows and storage bills climb.

The catalog becomes your critical dependency. It holds the single pointer, so its availability and its atomic swap decide your write safety. Pick one deliberately, and keep every engine on the same catalog.
Skip it for tiny tables or single-writer pipelines where plain Parquet is enough. And a stream of tiny commits fights optimistic concurrency. Batch the writes or buffer them upstream.

show.title: When not to use it
items: Streams of tiny commits: batch first

check.q: Why is the catalog choice an architectural decision?
opts: It stores all the data files
It holds the atomic pointer that guards write safety across engines
It decides the Parquet compression
check.why: The catalog's atomic pointer swap is what makes commits safe, so its availability and consistency bound the whole table.

work: Document which catalog all engines use and its failover plan.
Estimate monthly metadata growth and set maintenance schedules.
Review whether small tables really need Iceberg.

title: A table is a library catalogue

beats.say: How do you find one book among ten million without walking every shelf?

show.text: Find one book in ten million

beats.say: A library keeps a catalogue. Drawers point to cards, cards point to shelves. You open a few drawers, read a few cards, and walk straight to the right shelf.

chip.text: Read a little, skip the rest

beats.say: Iceberg does this for data files in cloud storage. Small metadata files say which data files hold which values, so a query reads only the files it needs.

chip.text: Only the needed files are opened

beats.say: And when someone adds books, the new catalogue goes live in one step. Readers see the old shelves or the new ones, never a half-finished mess.

check.q: Why can a query on an Iceberg table skip most of its files?
opts: It reads small metadata that says which files can match
It keeps every file in memory
It sorts the whole table before each query
check.why: The metadata records value ranges per file, so the engine can rule files out before opening them.

work: Find one slow lake table and count how many files a typical query opens.
Ask which of your tables several tools read, and whether each keeps its own copy.

title: The metadata tree, top to bottom

beats.say: A table has two million files. How does Iceberg plan a query without listing a single folder?
The catalog points to the current metadata file. That names the current snapshot, which points to a manifest list. Each manifest list row says which partition range one manifest covers.
Each manifest row describes one data file: its path, row count, and the minimum and maximum of every column. The planner drops manifests, then files, that cannot match the filter.
So planning reads a handful of small files instead of paging through millions of object listings.

check.q: What does a manifest file hold?
opts: One row per data file, with column minimums and maximums
The table schema history only
A copy of every row in the table
check.why: Manifests list data files with per-column statistics, which is what lets the planner skip files.

work: Query the files metadata table of a big table and look at file sizes.
Run rewrite_manifests when planning time creeps up.

title: Hidden partitioning and changing it later

beats.say: Why does a forgotten date filter scan a whole Hive table, but not an Iceberg one?
In Hive, users filter on a separate partition column. Forget it, and every file is read. Iceberg stores a transform instead, such as days of event time.
A filter on event time is turned into partition pruning automatically. Nobody needs to know the partition column even exists.
Each file also records the partition spec it was written with. Switch from daily to hourly, and only new files use hours. Old files stay put, and the planner reads both.

check.q: You change a table from daily to hourly partitions. What happens to old files?
opts: They keep their daily spec and are still pruned correctly
They must all be rewritten first
They become unreadable
check.why: Every file records its own partition spec, so evolution is a metadata change.

work: Look for Hive tables where analysts often forget the partition filter.
Pick partition transforms from the filters queries really use.

title: Two writers, one table

beats.say: Two jobs commit to the same table at the same second. Who wins, and what does a reader see?
Each writer writes its files and a new metadata file, then asks the catalog to swap the pointer, but only if it still points where it started. One swap wins.
The loser rereads the new state and checks for conflict. Two appends never clash, so it simply retries on top. Two jobs rewriting the same files do clash, and one fails.
A reader pins one snapshot when its query starts. It sees a whole commit or none of it, even while writes keep landing.

chip.text: All of a commit or none of it

check.q: Two jobs append new rows to one Iceberg table at the same time. What usually happens?
opts: One swap wins and the other retries on top and succeeds
Both commits are lost
The table locks until an admin steps in
check.why: Appends do not touch the same files, so the losing writer rebases on the new snapshot and commits.

work: Give each table one main writing job.
Alert on commit retries and commit failures per table.

title: Copy-on-write or merge-on-read

beats.say: Delete one row from a five hundred megabyte file. Should you rewrite the whole file?
Copy-on-write says yes. Every file holding a changed row is rewritten. Writes are slow and costly, but readers see only clean data files.
Merge-on-read writes a tiny delete file instead, naming the rows to drop. Writes are cheap, but every query must merge those deletes, and reads slow down as they pile up.
Pick copy-on-write for tables read all day and changed in nightly batches. Pick merge-on-read for constant small changes, like a CDC feed, and compact on a schedule.

check.q: A table gets CDC updates every minute and is read a few times an hour. Which mode fits?
opts: Merge-on-read with scheduled compaction
Copy-on-write
Neither: CDC cannot go into Iceberg
check.why: Frequent small changes make copy-on-write rewrite huge files constantly; merge-on-read keeps writes cheap and compaction keeps reads healthy.

work: Check the delete file count on your merge-on-read tables.
Set the write mode per table, not one default for all.

title: Small files and the snapshot bill

beats.say: You compacted the table. So why did storage go up?
A job writing every minute adds small files, a manifest and a snapshot each time. After a month, that is about forty three thousand snapshots and tens of thousands of tiny files.

show.title: After one month of minute commits

beats.say: Compaction writes big files and a new snapshot. But older snapshots still point to the small files for time travel, so nothing is freed until you expire them.
So schedule four jobs: compact data files, expire old snapshots, remove orphan files, and rewrite manifests. Retention is a business choice, because it limits how far back you can roll back.

check.q: Why does storage stay high right after compaction?
opts: Older snapshots still reference the small files
Compaction copies data twice on purpose
Object storage never frees space
check.why: Files are deleted only once no snapshot needs them, which is what expire_snapshots arranges.

work: Agree a snapshot retention period with the data owners.
Schedule compaction and expiry together in one maintenance DAG.
Track files per partition and average file size.

title: Should we put this on Iceberg?

beats.say: Leadership says: move every table to Iceberg. Do you say yes?
Say yes where several engines share data, like Spark writing and Trino and Snowflake reading, where storing and loading copies twice is costly, or where lock-in to one vendor is a real risk.
Compare honestly. Delta is smoothest inside Databricks. Hudi shines at heavy record upserts. A warehouse table needs no maintenance from you. Plain Parquet with Hive has no atomic commits.
Push back for small data one warehouse handles well, for row by row transactions, and when nobody will own compaction, snapshot expiry and the catalog.

check.q: Which situation is the strongest reason to choose Iceberg?
opts: Spark, Trino and Snowflake must share the same tables
One small team uses one warehouse for gigabytes of data
An app needs thousands of single-row updates a second
check.why: Iceberg pays off when several engines read and write one copy; the other two fit a warehouse or a database better.

work: Write a one-page decision note: engines, data size, owner, exit plan.
List which engine writes each candidate table.

title: Owning, paying and leaving Iceberg

beats.say: Who gets paged when an Iceberg table slows down?

A platform team owns the catalog, the maintenance jobs and the layout rules. Producing teams own each table schema. The catalog is the front door: it holds each table pointer and hands out storage access.
It fails as tiny files, piled up deletes, storage that never shrinks, commit clashes, and worst of all, two catalogs that both think they own a table. Show storage and compute cost per table.
Move off when one platform becomes the only engine and its native tables are cheaper, or when the work is really transactions. Then a warehouse table or a database is the better home.

check.q: What most often corrupts a shared Iceberg table?
opts: Two catalogs that both commit to it
Too many readers
Using hidden partitioning
check.why: Commits are atomic only within one catalog; two catalogs swapping different pointers lose each other’s changes.

work: Name the single catalog of record for every shared table.
Report storage and maintenance cost per table each month.
Review tables only one engine still uses.
